title: The Guru's alphabet
hookLine: Gurmukhi, from the Guru's mouth, has thirty-five letters and a set of vowel signs
last: YOUR RHYTHM — YOU CAN DO THIS.

cards: Plastic letters on a fridge door. A for apple, B for ball. Before a child can read a single word, they can make the sounds, and they'll say them to anyone who'll listen.
Today a new camp begins the same way, with letters. For the next seventy-five days, you and i will read one text together, slowly: Guru Nanak's Japji Sahib, the first hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib.
First, the script it's written in.

teach.b: The script is Gurmukhi. Gur is Guru; mukhi comes from mukh, the mouth. From the mouth of the Guru.
Sikhs trace it to Guru Angad, the second Guru, who, tradition says, shaped and settled the letters so the Sikhs could write down Guru Nanak's hymns.
The letters grew out of older scripts already used in Punjab; Guru Angad gave them a form, and a purpose.
The alphabet is called the painti, which simply means thirty-five, for its thirty-five basic letters.
It opens with three letters that carry vowels, oora, aira and eeree, then the consonants march in neat rows: sassa, haha, then kakka, khakha, gagga, and on.
Small vowel signs above, below and beside the letters change the sound.

Later, a handful of extra letters with a dot at the foot were added for sounds borrowed from Persian, so modern charts show a few more than thirty-five. Here's the gift for a learner: Gurmukhi is close to phonetic.
Mostly, you say what you see. So you can sound out Japji long before you understand it, the way a child sings a song before knowing what the words mean.
And, as you saw on day nine, the very first character of the Guru Granth Sahib isn't a letter at all.
It's the numeral one, joined to the letter oora, with a long curve sweeping over the top: Ik Onkar. The One, who is everywhere. The whole scripture begins with a number and a sound.
So in this camp, read with the mouth first. Understanding follows.

how: Sikh children often learn the Gurmukhi letters at gurdwara Punjabi classes, reciting the painti aloud, so that they can read Gurbani for themselves.

games.q: the Sikhs need to write down Guru Nanak's hymns. what does Guru Angad do, tradition says?
o: borrow a script from far away.
shape and settle the letters already used in Punjab.
games.why: he gave the local letters a settled form, and it became Gurmukhi, from the Guru's mouth.

practice: Look at Ik Onkar on the screen, lift one finger, and trace it slowly in the air, as if writing on a window: the numeral one, the round letter beside it, then the long curve that sweeps up over the top and keeps going.
Do it three times, a little smoother each time, saying Ik Onkar quietly if you pray. Then rest your hand in your lap, breathe, and let the shape stay behind your eyes.
